desync_detection_verified_live_and_the_n.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-18, two runs, one code change between them. Session research/sessions/session-20261018T0924Z-desync-verified. CONFIRMED, READER AND LOAD GATE: movement-ready fired at t+13.115 s (run 1) and t+14.488 s (run 2) after the first channel-1 record, with 1,342 channel-1 records in the session - inside the 8-14 s band predicted from the captured corpus, against a 60 s timer that cannot see the difference. REFUTED, THE FIRST DESIGN: the initial DesyncTracker compared the raw wire claim with the server's own position and argued in its own docstring that no offset was needed because they were 'the same quantity in the same frame of reference'. Run 1 refuted that: re-reading all 2,562 channel-1 claims over two minutes against the server's truth gave an error of EXACTLY 4.0311 u in EVERY sample, with a SINGLE distinct position (the player never moved). A perfectly in-sync player therefore sat permanently above the 2.0 u floor and was reported as desynced. That 4.0311 u is the instrument offset, matching the independently probe-measured (-2.200, +3.378). THE CORRECTION, now measured: the offset is calibrated per session with NO probe - at spawn the client is where the server put it, so the constant difference over the first samples IS the offset. Run 2 logged movement-calibrated offset (-2.2002, +3.3777), magnitude 4.0311 u, residual 0.0000 u, 20 samples, reproducing the probe measurement to four decimals from a different data path - and then NO movement-desync. A calibration whose samples are not tightly clustered is REJECTED, not averaged, because a wrong offset silently hides real divergence; and DesyncTracker FAILS OPEN while uncalibrated, returning IGNORE with an explicit 'uncalibrated' reason, since with the offset unknown a 4 u difference cannot be told from a real divergence. POSITIVE HALF ALSO CONFIRMED: with the offset fixed, W held 3 s (scripts/hold-key.py 'New World' 0x11 3) produced movement-desync error_u 3.342, streak 5, claim (9342.902, 2787.105) vs truth (9343.642, 2786.733) - real divergence, because the server's truth stays frozen at the spawn position. That is the honest shape of the current system: it detects that it has lost track of the player and cannot yet correct it. NOT ESTABLISHED: that the desync is corrected; correction is still spawn-only. GATE 6 TRAP RE-CONFIRMED: the first launch of this session reached InGame but never streamed (0 Slice lines, black screen, no channel-1 record, OnLocalNetworkConnectionWarning 1->4) because az.py dev was started without AZOTH_REPLAY_LOCAL_PLAYER_UUID=character, whose default is the failing value.

position_fragment_located_and_a_minimal_.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-18, two results. (1) THE POSITION FRAGMENT IS LOCATED FROM THE CLIENT. The 46393-byte spawn payload is 48 fragments whose boundaries are NOT derivable from the bytes (a fragment has no length field; its payload length is implied by its type; the spawn record's first fragment is type 4878, outside the nine types the 7154-byte record gave us). `python az.py probe frida-fragment-grammar --min-fragments 20` captured the same 48 offsets 25 times, byte-identical: 2, 25, 171, 280, 320, 6233 ... 46286, 46304. THE POSITION IS IN FRAGMENT #35, payload offset 38310..38397, header `10 0b` = key 16 type 11 - the same key/type as fragment #6 of the 7154-byte player record. The replay store's 24 captured copies carry a BYTE-IDENTICAL fragment #35 (only the value differs). That yields a 101-byte record-1 bundle (103 with the rewritten counter), 451x smaller than the 46407-byte spawn record, round-tripping as record_id=1 fragment_count=1. (2) SENDING IT ALONE DOES NOT REPOSITION THE PLAYER, and this is the negative that closes the line: with the minimal bundle wired to the correction path, the player walked, error grew to 3.186 u, `movement-desync` fired, the 102-byte correction was sent, the client reported 0 `Failed to unmarshal` / 0 `ValidationError` / 0 `transportError`, the character stayed VISIBLE (the full-spawn-record attempt had made it invisible) - and the error then GREW to 16.5 u and stayed there. A record-1 bundle with a single fragment is not a repositioning message; the client appears to need the record's full fragment set, consistent with the full spawn record having moved the player at spawn (0.0000 u, 2026-10-14). So the position is LOCATABLE but not ADDRESSABLE as a standalone message with today's knowledge; the remaining question is whether the client treats the record as an atomic unit, which is a decompilation question. PROBE DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED: frida-fragment-grammar read the record's out_u16 in the record reader's onLeave and attached it to each fragment event, but fragments are emitted in the fragment reader's onLeave which runs BEFORE the record's - all 300 previously captured fragment events carried recordId null, so the docstring's claim that every fragment event carries the record id was false. It now buffers and emits at record leave, and filters by fragment count, which is required anyway because the spawn record and the player metadata record are BOTH record_id 1 (48 vs 9 fragments). TWO DEFECTS OF MINE, both caught only by live measurement: (a) the correction body was a SimpleNamespace while `_send_state_bundle` calls dataclasses.replace(), raising TypeError that the UDP loop swallowed and that killed the session with a client transportError 4 - fixed by using ReplayMessage, with a test asserting is_dataclass(); (b) the cap check logged on every sample, hundreds of lines a second. AZOTH_MOVEMENT_CORRECT defaults to 0.

record_dispatcher_gates_updates_and_the_.what: STATIC, first-hand, 2026-10-18, decompiled to explain the live negative `position_fragment_located_and_a_minimal_bundle_does_not_move_the_player_20261018`. THE CALL SITE (confirmed in the decompiled caller, matching the atlas note): FUN_14175ccc0 loops over the bundle's records, calls FUN_146af20d0(&reader, &out_record_id, &fragment_vector) for each, and then calls FUN_141717fc0(state, out_record_id, &fragment_vector, *FUN_1406d97b0(msg), byte[msg+8], lVar14, FUN_1406c10a0(msg)) - i.e. the record id, the fragment vector, the message SEQ, a FLAG BYTE at msg+8, the reader's success value, and the clientContextInstanceId. THE APPLY GATE (line 504 of the decompiled body): `if ((param_5 == '�') || (puVar24 = puStack_2c8, uVar11 == 0)) { ... }` where uVar11 is the record's existing handler slot `*(state + 0x608 + record_id*0x10)`. So an update is applied only when the flag byte at msg+8 is ZERO **or** the record's slot was EMPTY. A record whose slot already exists and whose msg+8 is non-zero is silently skipped - no error, no effect. That is the shape of the measured failure: the 102-byte correction produced 0 `Failed to unmarshal`, 0 `ValidationError`, 0 `transportError` and no movement. THE FIRST FRAGMENT SELECTS THE PATH (line 207): immediately after the slot lookup the dispatcher performs a VIRTUAL CALL derived from the FIRST element of the fragment vector (`cVar5 = (**(code **)(**(longlong **)(*plStackX_18 + 8) + 0x60))();`) and branches on its result. The two branches differ: the `cVar5 != 0` branch contains an explicit `record_id == 1` special case (`auStackX_10[0] == 1`) guarded by another virtual predicate at `puVar24[0x10a] + 0x20`, and both branches end in `FUN_14178db00(state, *slot + 0x860, &value)`, which is the actual apply. CONSEQUENCE: the record is not treated as an unordered bag of fragments - the FIRST fragment's type decides how the record is handled. A 1-fragment record whose only fragment is the position (key 16 type 11) therefore does not take the same path as the 48-fragment spawn record, whose first fragment is key 71 type 4878. NOT CLAIMED: which specific virtual function slot 0x60 is, or what value msg+8 carries. Both need a targeted follow-up; the hypothesis they suggest is testable without more RE - compose record 1 with the spawn record's FIRST fragment plus the position fragment and see whether the client applies it.

the_record_flag_byte_selects_the_gate_an.va: 0x14643e7b0 (GameMessagePort handler) decompiled to reverse/builds/8654f01d.../functions/14643e7b0-14643f020.c; the flag byte is byte[msg+8] = the Carrier record flags; our sender is rep.py::_send_replay_message
the_record_flag_byte_selects_the_gate_an.what: STATIC, first-hand, 2026-10-18, and it resolves the `byte[msg+8]` question the record dispatcher raised. In FUN_14643e7b0 the state-bundle path branches on `*(char *)(msg + 8)`, which is the Carrier RECORD's FLAG BYTE (our MessageRecord.flags / flags_override; MessageFlags: RELIABLE 0x01, CHUNKS 0x04, SEQUENTIAL_ID 0x08, SEQUENTIAL_REL_ID 0x10, DATA_CHANNEL 0x20, NO_LENGTH 0x40, CONNECTING 0x80). TWO PATHS, and they are not equivalent: (a) `byte[msg+8] == 0` -> calls FUN_14175ccc0 directly, i.e. the RELIABLE path, and does NOT touch `port + 0x78`; (b) otherwise -> the UNRELIABLE replication gate: `instanceId == port[0x80]` AND (`seq == port[0x78]` OR (`seq != -1` AND (`port[0x78] == -1` OR `port[0x78] < seq`))) -> then `port[0x78] = seq` and FUN_14175ccc0, else the message is DROPPED with the `MayHandleReplicationUnreliable() returning false` diagnostic. So the flag byte chooses between a path that leaves the replication high-water untouched and one that advances it. WHAT WE SEND: `_send_replay_message` sends every state bundle with `flags_override=0x21` (RELIABLE|DATA_CHANNEL), or 0x25 (RELIABLE|CHUNKS|DATA_CHANNEL) when chunked. The client's own capture has its state bundles at **flags 0x20** (DATA_CHANNEL only, i.e. UNRELIABLE). Consequence, and it is the leading explanation for the measured correction failures: by sending the reliable flag we take path (a) and never advance the client's replication high-water, so the client's notion of the latest replicated state does not move with our corrections, while every captured bundle it applies came through path (b). NOT YET TESTED: sending the correction with flags 0x20 and a strictly increasing seq, which is the form the capture uses and the only one that both advances the high-water and takes the dispatcher path. This is the next one-variable experiment.

correction_refuted_in_three_shapes_and_t.va: rep.py::_send_replay_message (flags), minimal_position_bundle, player_body_with_position_fragment, _queue_movement_correction; serve_forever error handlers; sessions session-20261018T1200Z-hybrid-correction-negative and the 13:00 run
correction_refuted_in_three_shapes_and_t.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-18. **Position correction is refuted in every shape tried, and one of the refutations also produced a real bug fix in the server.** THREE SHAPES, ALL SAFE, NONE APPLIED: (1) the full spawn record looped at 1 Hz, 46408 B - made the local character INVISIBLE; (2) the position fragment alone, 102 B - accepted, visible, no effect; (3) the 7154-byte record-1 composition the client demonstrably applies PLUS the position fragment, 7255 B, record_id=1 fragment_count=10 - accepted, visible, no effect. The third was sent TWICE, once with the reliable flag 0x21 and once with the unreliable 0x20 (the form the capture uses), because the decompiled FUN_14643e7b0 shows the flag byte selecting between a path that does not advance `port[0x78]` and one that does. BOTH failed identically: error grew past the correction (11.861 u and rising) with 0 `Failed to unmarshal`, 0 `ValidationError`, 0 `transportError`, character visible. So neither composition nor the flag byte is the obstacle. **A REAL PRE-EXISTING BUG WAS FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY, and it was killing sessions.** Three consecutive runs failed to reach the world; the server armed the replay and went silent, and its log ended with `UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'traceback' where it is not associated with a value` raised from the TICK-ERROR handler. That converted 'one bad datagram' into 'the world process dies' - the exact failure both handlers exist to prevent, and a plausible contributor to the intermittent `transportError 4` sessions recorded earlier in this project. Fixed by deleting the local import (the module-level one at line 36 is sufficient); with the fix in place the same handlers log properly and the server survived a full session. A SECOND bug of mine was caught by the new tests: `_send_replay_message` had its body edited to read `flags` while its SIGNATURE still said `(self, server, msg)`, so every replay send raised `NameError: name 'flags' is not defined` in the tick loop (104 tick errors, 46 client re-registrations, never reached the world). the_two_apply_paths_and_the_per_fragment.va: 0x141717fc0 (record dispatcher) decompiled in full; 0x1415e68b0 (component map insert/lookup); compare FUN_14178db00 (creation apply) vs the vtable+0x10 path (update apply)
the_two_apply_paths_and_the_per_fragment.what:
STATIC, first-hand, 2026-10-18, decompiled to answer why a record the client parses is not applied. **The dispatcher has TWO apply paths and they are structurally different.** PATH A, CREATION (slot `*(state + 0x608 + record_id*0x10)` was EMPTY): builds a value struct and calls `FUN_14178db00(state, *slot + 0x860, &value)` - one apply for the whole record. PATH B, UPDATE (slot already exists - the case for a correction, because the spawn already created it): it loops over the fragment vector, and for EACH fragment calls a VIRTUAL PREDICATE at `fragment->vtable + 0x60`; only when that predicate returns 0 does the fragment enter the component map `FUN_1415e68b0(state+0x578, ...)`. Fragments whose predicate returns non-zero are SKIPPED. After the loop it goes through `vtable + 0x10` on the record's handler object, and applies through THAT object's `+0x18`. `FUN_1415e68b0` was decompiled and is a hash map insert/lookup keyed on the fragment's key (`*(param_2+1)` is the 'inserted' flag) - it is the COMPONENT MAP, not the applier. CONSEQUENCE, and it is the answer: **the apply path is per-fragment and gated by a predicate the server does not control.** A correction is an UPDATE, so it must pass that predicate for the position fragment; the measured behaviour (accepted, zero errors, no effect) is exactly what a fragment that fails or is skipped by that predicate looks like. It also explains why the spawn record works: it arrives when the slot is EMPTY, so it takes PATH A, which applies the whole record with no per-fragment filter. NOT CLAIMED: what the predicate at `vtable + 0x60` actually tests, and whether the position fragment can ever satisfy it. That requires resolving which component type owns that vtable, which is the next targeted question - and it is why sending more payload shapes cannot work: the filter is not about the bytes we send.

CORRECTION 2026-10-18 (runtime, same day): the 'per-fragment filter' reading was WRONG. A live probe read the vtable the dispatcher actually calls and resolved the +0x60 slot: it is `xor al, al; ret` at VA 0x140294910, i.e. **it returns 0 unconditionally**, so the `if (cVar5 == '�')` branch is ALWAYS taken and every fragment is processed. There is no per-fragment filter. See `component_map_is_first_write_wins_20261018` for the mechanism that actually explains the refuted corrections.

fragment_object_vtable_identification_FA.va: 0x148582d50 (candidate vtable, +0x60 = 0x140878870, +0x58 = 0x14087bcc0, +0x90 = 0x1408733f0); 0x141717fc0 call site at the fragment loop
fragment_object_vtable_identification_FA.what: NEGATIVE RESULT, 2026-10-18. I tried to identify the vtable behind the per-fragment call in the dispatcher's UPDATE path, `cVar5 = (**(code **)(*(longlong *)plVar8[1] + 0x60))()` followed by `if (cVar5 == '�')`, in order to learn what the filter tests. THE IDENTIFICATION FAILED and is recorded so it is not repeated. What I did: located a vtable in .rdata whose slot +0x60 holds 0x140878870, and decompiled the neighbouring slots. What that showed is that it is NOT the fragment object's vtable:   +0x60 = 0x140878870 -> `read(n)`: takes the cursor at `this+0x28`, advances it by n, returns the PREVIOUS position. It returns a pointer/offset, NOT a bool, so it cannot be the `char` the dispatcher tests.   +0x58 = 0x14087bcc0 -> `write`: calls vtable+0x48 for a position then memcpy's the buffer into it.   +0x90 = 0x1408733f0 -> not a .pdata function start; the range decompiles into AZ reflection/allocator helpers (FUN_140873490 touches `_DAT_14a313ff8`, the AZ reflection registry singleton). So 0x148582d50 is a SERIALIZER/reader vtable, not the per-fragment object's. The correct next method is to obtain the vtable at runtime (the object is created inside FUN_146af2340 via a factory returned by `func_0x0001406d97d0(msg)` and stored at vector element +0x8), rather than by pattern-matching .rdata for a slot value. WHAT STILL STANDS from the same session and does not depend on this identification: the dispatcher has TWO structurally different apply paths (creation applies the whole record in one call; update loops per fragment and gates each one through a virtual call whose result must be 0), the component map FUN_1415e68b0 is a hash map keyed on the fragment key and is not the applier, and a correction always takes the UPDATE path because the spawn already created the slot. That is why four payload shapes failed identically: the gate is not about the bytes.

component_map_is_first_write_wins_202610.va: 0x1415e5140 and 0x1415e68b0 (fragment-key hash maps); 0x140294910 (the +0x60 slot, `xor al,al; ret`); probe reverse/probes/client/frida-fragment-vtable.py; capture .azoth/captures/probes/frag-vtable.jsonl
component_map_is_first_write_wins_202610.what: MEASURED AT RUNTIME 2026-10-18, and it is the mechanism that explains every refuted correction. METHOD: a new read-only probe hooked `FUN_141717fc0` on enter and walked the fragment vector it receives, reporting per fragment the key, the object pointer and its vtable. 400 records captured, including 25 spawn records (48 fragments) and 63 local-player records (9 fragments) - both `record_id 1`, told apart by count. FINDING 1, the +0x60 slot is not a filter. The slot is identical for EVERY fragment of EVERY record (0x7ff602ad4910 with base 0x7ff602840000 -> RVA 0x294910). Disassembled it is `xor al, al; ret` - it returns 0 unconditionally, so `if (cVar5 == '�')` is always taken and every fragment is processed. The earlier static reading of a 'per-fragment predicate that the server does not control' is REFUTED. FINDING 2, the maps are FIRST-WRITE-WINS. Both `FUN_1415e5140` (called per fragment with the fragment key) and `FUN_1415e68b0` are the same shape: hash on the key, walk the bucket, and `if (*param_3 == (int)puVar9[2]) { *(undefined1 *)(param_2 + 1) = 0; return existing; }` - an ALREADY PRESENT key is NOT replaced, and the caller receives the existing entry. So a fragment whose key the client already holds is DISCARDED. FINDING 3, key 16 (the position) carries the SAME vtable in both records (0x7ff60a93f900), but a DIFFERENT +0x90 reader than every other fragment (0x142a436b0 vs 0x1417b4110), so it is a distinct component type - consistent with it being the position-bearing component. WHY THIS EXPLAINS EVERYTHING MEASURED: the spawn record is sent when the keys are ABSENT, so every fragment is inserted - which is why the 2026-10-14 spawn-position override worked with 0.0000 u error. Every later correction re-sends key 16, which is ALREADY PRESENT, so it is discarded and the client keeps the spawn value. That is exactly the measured behaviour: accepted with zero errors, character visible, position unchanged. CONSEQUENCE for a real fix: a correction must first REMOVE the component (the AOI trait registry already contains `replica_portrayal_remove`) or use a delta/update message rather than re-sending the fragment. Re-sending a key cannot work by construction.

the_position_is_spawn_only_in_replicated.va: record_id 1 of the type-0x08 bundle; spawn variant = 48 fragments / 46393 B payload (seq 0x2a..0x6c); ongoing player variant = 9 fragments / 7154 B (seq 0x98/0x9a/0x9c/0x9e); fragment key=16 type=11 in both
the_position_is_spawn_only_in_replicated.what:
MEASURED 2026-10-18 over the committed replay (29 record-1 bundles) and it closes the position-authority question with a structural answer rather than another experiment. THE TWO VARIANTS OF record_id 1: 24 bundles carry **48 fragments / 46393 B** and are the SPAWN record; 5 bundles carry **9 fragments / 7154 B** and are the client's ONGOING player state - the ones the state stream re-sends at 4 Hz and the ones that keep the player simulating. THE POSITION IS ONLY IN THE SPAWN VARIANT: all 24 spawn bundles contain the x/y pair; NONE of the 5 ongoing-player bundles do. Both variants carry fragment `key=16 type=11` with the SAME vtable (0x7ff60a93f900, same component type) but with DIFFERENT payload sizes - 85 B in the spawn (position at payload offset 20) vs 49 B in the player record (no position at all). So the component has optional/variant fields and the position is one of them, present only in the spawn encoding. WHY THIS IS THE ANSWER, and it explains every measurement in this project at once: (a) the 2026-10-14 spawn override moved the client to the server's value with **0.0000 u** error, because the spawn variant does carry the pair; (b) re-sending the spawn record cannot update it later, because the component map is first-write-wins (`component_map_is_first_write_wins_20261018`); (c) the 4 Hz stream cannot update it either, because the ongoing variant does not carry the position at all - so no amount of streaming, and no payload composition, can move the player through record-1; (d) the player nonetheless moves freely, because the client PREDICTS locally. CONCLUSION: in replicated state the position is SPAWN-ONLY BY DESIGN. The ongoing position is client-authoritative and server correction has to travel on the dedicated channel - `ReceivePlayerPositionClientMsg` (4216) -> `IPositionReceiver` - which this build never instantiates (installer 0, register 0, 0 of 225 vtables over 37,063 targets, measured 2026-10-12). That is why 'the server owns the player's position over time' is unreachable via state bundles and why four payload shapes failed identically. This also matches the vendor's own account of the design: the client predicts and stretches the animation, the server is authoritative and sends the outcome back - which requires a working correction channel, not a replicated field.

CORRECTION 2026-10-18 (later the same day): the phrase 'SPAWN-ONLY BY DESIGN' was an overreach. The capture used to prove it is a session in which the player NEVER MOVED - the x/y pair is byte-identical across all 24 spawn records, so it could not contain a correction. What IS solid and unchanged: the ongoing player-state variant (9 fragments) does not carry the pair, and the component map is first-write-wins. What is NOT solid: any claim about how the original server corrected a desync, because no capture in this repository contains one. See `the_design_is_client_prediction_plus_server_validation_20261018`.

ipositionreceiver_apply_is_a_stub_so_the.va: interface vtable 0x1482eb160 (only vtable carrying QI 0x143fadd00); slot +0x40 = 0x140294860 = `ret 0`; delivery 0x143f97bf0; QI 0x143fadd00; descriptor 0x1482ea920
ipositionreceiver_apply_is_a_stub_so_the.what: STATIC, first-hand, 2026-10-18 (Steam exe 8654f01d, image base 0x140000000), and it CLOSES the position-correction question: **the method the delivery calls to apply a position is an unimplemented stub, so this channel cannot work regardless of target binding.** WHAT THE DELIVERY DOES (decompiled 0x143f97bf0): `target = FUN_1416bcba0(); if (target) { qi = target->vtable[0x20](target, IPositionReceiver_guid); if (qi) { read 4 u32 at msg+0x30 and a u64 at msg+0x40; qi->vtable[0x40](qi, that_u64, &those_floats); return 1; } } return 0;` So the APPLY is `vtable[0x40]` on the object QI returned. THE STUB: the interface vtable is **0x1482eb160**, and its slot **+0x40 = 0x140294860**, which disassembles to exactly `c2 00 00` = `ret 0`. Slots +0x48, +0x50 and +0x58 are the same stub. Neighbouring slots ARE implemented (+0x30 = `jmp 0x143fa8520`, +0x38 = a real function with a prologue), so the interface is live but THIS method is not. NO OTHER VTABLE CARRIES THE QI: searching all of .rdata for the QI pointer 0x143fadd00 yields exactly **2 occurrences, both inside 0x1482eb160** (its +0x20 and +0x28 slots). There is therefore NO static concrete-class vtable with the QI at +0x20 and a real function at +0x40. Any implementation would have to be built at runtime through AZ reflection - and the measured session found installer=0 and register=0 for a whole login + world entry + 18 minutes (`position_receiver_never_created_in_a_full_session_20261012`). TWO EARLIER MEASUREMENTS ARE EXPLAINED BY THIS: the 'delivery succeeded 260/260 non-null' in `position_reply_target_fixes_dispatch_20261011` was measuring this stub (the delivery returns 1 unconditionally once QI succeeds, whether or not anything was applied), and the scan finding 'no registered target answers the interface' (`position_target_scan_no_binding_20261011`) is consistent with there being no implementation to bind. THE MESSAGE LAYOUT THE DELIVERY EXPECTS, recorded for completeness: x,y,z and a fourth u32 at msg+0x30/0x34/0x38/0x3c, plus a u64 at msg+0x40. CONCLUSION: `ReceivePlayerPositionClientMsg` (4216) -> `IPositionReceiver` is a DEAD END in this build, and it is NOT a binding problem. Unblocking it would require a runtime-built implementation that the shipped client never creates. Server authority over the local player's ongoing position is therefore not reachable through any channel measured in this project: not replicated state (spawn-only, first-write-wins) and not this RMI (stub).

the_design_is_client_prediction_plus_ser.va: cvars recovered from the exe: javelin.alc-correct-position-desync-during-attack-slow-down, javelin.alc-correct-lateral-desyncs-during-attack-slow-down, javelin-server.alc-speed-hack-fix-v2-enabled/-wipe-inputs/-max-buffered-inputs/-clamp-buffer-grace-counter, javelin-server.player-teleport-2d-distance-metrics-threshold, javelin-server.player-teleport-instant-aoi-radius-threshold, javelin.alc-validate-sector-bounds, javelin.num-inputs-to-wait-for, javelin-server.ALC-max-input-to-combine, javelin-server.alc-request-input-throttle-server-override-delay-ms, javelin-server.process-input-end-of-timeslice, javelin-server.positionalticketing-*; implementation services/world/src/azoth_world/movement.py::MovementSimulator
the_design_is_client_prediction_plus_ser.what: RECOVERED 2026-10-18 from the client's own cvar names, and it settles how the original handled movement authority - without needing a capture of a moving player, which this repository does not have. **THE CLIENT IS AUTHORITATIVE OVER ITS OWN LOCOMOTION; THE SERVER VALIDATES AND REACTS.** The cvar prefixes say exactly that: the correction cvars are `javelin.alc-correct-*` (CLIENT-side: the client corrects its own desync), while the server-side cvars are all VALIDATION and INPUT CONTROL (`javelin-server.alc-speed-hack-fix-v2-*` including `-wipe-inputs`, `player-teleport-2d-distance-metrics-threshold`, `alc-validate-sector-bounds`, `num-inputs-to-wait-for`, `ALC-max-input-to-combine`, `alc-request-input-throttle-*`, `process-input-end-of-timeslice`). CONSEQUENCE, and it invalidates the search this project spent effort on: **there is no server-to-client position-push message to find.** The server's leverage is (a) validating the client's reported movement against speed/teleport/sector rules, and (b) controlling the input buffer - how many inputs it accepts, whether it throttles them, and whether it wipes them. A 'correction' is the server refusing or dropping inputs, after which the CLIENT reconciles. That is why `SetInputsThrottled` exists only as a ServerFacet message (the client reporting to the server) and why no ClientFacet counterpart exists. IMPLEMENTED as `movement.MovementSimulator`: it holds the server's OWN position, seeded at spawn (where the server genuinely decides), folds in the client's validated claims, and HOLDS its own value when a claim is implausible. The step is measured against the server's position rather than the client's previous claim, because `MovementValidator` resets its reference on a rejected teleport - measuring there would refuse a teleport once and then accept it, letting an insisting client win after a single refusal. `AZOTH_STATE_POSITION=sim` publishes the simulated position into the state the server sends, so the position the server reports is computed rather than replayed.

the_input_stream_carries_the_clients_mov.what: DECODED 2026-10-18 from the client's own input stream, over 34 distinct positions in one session. The channel-1 body carries a run of big-endian float32 immediately after the `3d 4c cc cd` marker (the float 0.05):   payload 119 = body 91 : marker 0.05   +4   float32 a    -2.93 .. +0.33   (varies with movement; MEANING NOT ESTABLISHED)   +8   float32 b    -0.01 .. +0.18   (idem)   +12  float32 x    world x   +16  float32 y    world y   +20  float32      zero while walking (NOT z; the wire carries a 2D position)   +24  float32      zero VERIFIED: x and y here equal the pair the position claim reports, to within 0.01 u, **34 of 34** distinct positions, and a second pass through the reader over **201 samples** gave 0 mismatches. So the client reports its position twice in the same body, and this is the block a server needs in order to predict. OFFSETS: measured on the PAYLOAD (119). The reader works on the BODY, which starts 28 bytes later, so the marker is at body offset 91. Both constants are recorded because mixing them is an easy mistake; the reader locates the block with `find()` rather than by index, so a wrong constant cannot silently read the wrong bytes. NOT CLAIMED: what `a` and `b` mean. They vary with movement and would be the natural velocity/heading candidates, but nothing has established that, so they are exposed as raw floats and the predictive simulator estimates velocity from consecutive server-held positions instead of inventing a meaning for them.

the_server_predicts_then_checks_20261018.what: IMPLEMENTED 2026-10-18. `MovementSimulator` adopts a validated claim - the server ends up holding whatever the client said. `PredictiveSimulator` derives its OWN expected position: it estimates a velocity from consecutive server-held positions, predicts the next one, and records how far the client's claim was from that prediction (`PredictionCheck`), while still adopting the claim when it is plausible. That distinction is the point: the client stays authoritative over its locomotion - which is what the cvar names say the original design does - but the server now has an INDEPENDENT expectation, so it can say 'that step does not follow from what you reported' rather than only 'that step was too fast'. MEASURED on a synthetic 3 s walk at 5 u/s with 0.05 u of noise: 60 samples, 0 violations, 0 disagreements, mean prediction error 0.0654 u, estimated velocity 4.617 u/s. Then a 900 u teleport in one sample: refused with 'teleport from the server's position: 884.993 u' and the server kept its own position. ON REAL CAPTURED DATA the simulator was fed 2001 claims and reported 0 violations and 0 prediction error - because that dump is a session in which the player never moved, which is itself the confirmation that the quiet case is quiet. The velocity estimate is a placeholder for `a`/`b` in the movement block: when those are decoded they can be substituted without changing this interface.

the_movement_block_a_is_the_camera_yaw_a.what:
DECODED 2026-10-18 over **1008 measured displacements** in six sessions, and the first hypothesis was REFUTED by the measurement. `a` IS THE CAMERA YAW (radians, wrapped to [-pi, pi]). Established by classifying every displacement by `(movement heading - a)`:   strafe left  (+90 deg) 47.8%   back         (+180)    24.4%   strafe right (-90)     11.8%   forward      (0)        5.4% That is the signature of WASD movement relative to a camera. The competing reading - that `a` is the direction of travel - fits only 5.4% and is refuted; it was tried first and the histogram killed it. `b` REMAINS UNKNOWN and is exposed raw. It correlates with POSITION rather than with speed or heading (corr(speed, b) = -0.0095), stays inside [-0.53, +0.46], and has 637 distinct values, so it is not speed, not a heading, and not a small angle. `a` is therefore USABLE and `b` is not: a server can turn a camera yaw plus a movement intent into a world direction, and cannot do that with `b` until `b` is decoded. IMPLEMENTED as `YawAwareSimulator`: it predicts from consecutive server-held positions and decomposes the resulting velocity into forward (along the yaw) and lateral (across it), so the server can say HOW the player is moving, not just how fast. MEASURED on 3001 real captured samples: 10 violations, 4 prediction disagreements, mean prediction error **0.0334 u**, yaw captured on 2990 of them. NOT YET: prediction from INTENT. That needs which keys are held, and the input stream has not been shown to carry it - the yaw plus a finite-difference velocity is the precondition, not the answer.

UPDATE 2026-10-18 (same session): **`b` IS ALSO DECODED - it is the camera PITCH.** The earlier note that it stayed unknown was written before the second measurement. Evidence, by the same method that established the yaw: `b` has 637 distinct values but changes only **770 times in 197810 samples** (mean run 256), exactly like the yaw's 729 changes at run 271 - so it is HELD camera state, not per-sample movement data. Its range is [-30.3 deg, +26.1 deg], a pitch range. And **691 of the 808 angle changes are SIMULTANEOUS in `a` and `b`** (turning the mouse diagonally), with 38 yaw-only and 79 pitch-only changes (looking up or down). Correlations against speed, forward speed and lateral speed are all below 0.10, which is what an independent camera angle looks like. So the block is **(pitch, yaw, x, y)**: the client's camera orientation and its world position in one sample. The pitch is recorded but NOT used in the velocity decomposition, because the wire carries a 2D position - z is derived by the client - so movement happens in the plane and a pitch cannot contribute to it. Inventing a vertical component would be exactly the kind of unverified inference this project keeps paying for.

REFINED 2026-10-18 with the live movement feed: **the yaw is measured from +Y, not from +X.** Over 79 displacements during a real walk, `(movement heading - yaw)` is **+90.0 deg** in 77 of them and +90..+105 in the other 2 - a CONSTANT, not a distribution. So the forward direction is `(-sin(yaw), cos(yaw))`, which at the measured yaw of -154.04 deg gives (0.438, -0.899) - exactly the direction the player actually walked. Using `(cos, sin)` - the obvious reading - reports a player walking forward as walking SIDEWAYS by 90 deg, and it was measured doing exactly that before this fix: forward_speed 0.00 / lateral 3.83 on a plain forward walk. Corrected: forward 3.83 / lateral 0.00.

the_movement_block_is_pitch_yaw_x_y_2026.what: FINAL DECODE 2026-10-18 of the channel-1 movement block, over 197810 samples and 1008 measured displacements. The block is FOUR big-endian float32 after the `0.05` marker:   +4  pitch   [-30.3 deg, +26.1 deg]   camera pitch   +8  yaw     [-179.5 deg, +179.9]     camera yaw   +12 x                                world x   +16 y                                world y ESTABLISHED BY: (a) the yaw by the distribution of (movement heading - yaw) over 1008 displacements - 47.8% at +90 deg (strafe left), 24.4% at +180 (back), 11.8% at -90 (strafe right), 5.4% at 0 (forward), i.e. WASD against a camera; the 'direction of travel' reading fits 5.4% and is refuted. (b) the pitch by held-ness and range: 770 changes in 197810 samples (mean run 256, like the yaw's 729/271), range [-30.3, +26.1] deg, and 691 of 808 angle changes simultaneous with the yaw while 79 are pitch-only. USED: `YawAwareSimulator` decomposes the observed velocity into forward (along the yaw) and lateral (across it), so the server reports HOW the player moves. The pitch is recorded and deliberately NOT used: the wire carries a 2D position, so movement is planar and a pitch cannot contribute. MEASURED on 4001 real captured samples with yaw and pitch: 29 violations, 8 prediction disagreements, mean prediction error 0.0419 u, orientation captured on 3971 of them. STILL NOT: prediction from INTENT. The block gives orientation and position, not which keys are held, so the server can interpret a movement but cannot yet originate one.

movement_intent_is_not_decodable_from_th.va: channel-1 type 0x635 body, 311-byte payload; corpus services/world/rep_traffic.jsonl (172575 samples scanned)
movement_intent_is_not_decodable_from_th.what:
BLOCKED, 2026-10-18, and the blocker is DATA, not analysis. I set out to find the movement INTENT (which keys are held) in the channel-1 body, which is the last piece needed for the server to originate a movement instead of only interpreting one. WHAT THE BODY OFFERS: only **34 of 283 body bytes ever vary**. Their ranges are body 17..51 (before the movement block), the movement block itself (96..112), and four 2-byte counters at 122/163/204/245. Two bytes are binary and were the obvious intent candidates: body 17 (0 in 5427 samples, 1 in 573) and body 58 (1 in 5164, 0 in 836). WHY IT CANNOT BE DECIDED: correlating any of them with movement needs samples where the client actually MOVES, and the corpus does not contain them. Scanning all 172575 channel-1 samples in services/world/rep_traffic.jsonl for consecutive-sample displacement gives   > 0.01 u : 2 pairs   > 0.05 u : 2 pairs   > 0.10 u : 2 pairs   > 0.30 u : 0 pairs   > 1.00 u : 0 pairs Two pairs is not a sample. An earlier pass that grouped by distinct POSITION looked like movement (355 distinct positions in one session) but that is the client drifting while standing, not locomotion: the per-sample displacement is essentially zero. A first correlation attempt reported 'no difference' between flag=0 and flag=1 groups; that result is NOT evidence either way, because both groups were almost entirely stationary (mean speed 0.001 u/sample). Reporting it as a negative would have been wrong. WHAT IS NEEDED: a session in which the player WALKS CONTINUOUSLY for tens of seconds while the traffic log captures channel 1. The existing captures cannot answer this question at any level of analysis, so no further static work will unblock it. WHAT DOES NOT DEPEND ON THIS: the server already has its own position, its own prediction (mean error 0.0419 u on 4001 real samples), a rejection criterion that holds against an insisting client, and the player's frame from the camera yaw and pitch. Prediction from intent would let it originate a movement; everything else is already there.

RESOLVED THE DATA PROBLEM, 2026-10-18: a live session was captured in which the player walked continuously (W held 24 s, six holds of 4 s). The player DID move - from (9341.44, 2790.11) to (9251.20, 3015.70), over 240 u - and the input stream recorded it. BUT THE POSITION IS NOT CONTINUOUS: over 5128 samples there are only **3 position changes**, and they are JUMPS of 42.866, 157.105 and 128.797 u. Between them the reported position is byte-identical for hundreds of samples. WHAT THAT MEANS: the channel-1 position is not a per-frame sample of a walking player. It is updated in bursts, so the input stream cannot be used to reconstruct a continuous trajectory at 20 Hz - and the intent flags cannot be correlated against per-sample displacement, because there IS no per-sample displacement to correlate against. WHAT WAS LEARNED ANYWAY: the movement block's x,y DOES change on each of the three jumps, so the block is genuinely the position and it travels with the update. And of the bytes that differ across a jump, the ranges are consistent: 0..3 (the container CRC), 53..54, 71/73, 78..79, 86..87 (a small counter), the movement block 123..140, and four 2-byte counters at 150/191/232/273. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SERVER: prediction between claims has to come from the CAMERA ORIENTATION and the validator, not from an interpolated position history - which is exactly what `YawAwareSimulator` already does. The measured prediction error (0.0419 u on 4001 samples) was computed on a session where the position never changed, so it measures the quiet case, not a walk. NEXT, IF INTENT IS WANTED: it needs a session captured while the player walks AND a way to see the per-frame state - either a client-side probe reading the position accessor at 20 Hz, or a different message the client sends while moving. The channel-1 stream alone does not carry it.

the_channel_one_position_is_a_spawn_anch.va: channel-1 type 0x635 body offset 131/135 (payload); probe reverse/probes/client/frida-player-position.py; capture .azoth/captures/probes/player-position-1792357020.jsonl
the_channel_one_position_is_a_spawn_anch.what:
MEASURED 2026-10-18 with the decisive instrument: the client's OWN position accessor polled at 20 Hz (`frida-player-position`, which calls `FUN_140fddfa0` exactly as the client's `nw_getPlayerPosition` command does) WHILE the player walked, correlated against the channel-1 claim from the traffic log. THE WALK WAS REAL: the accessor recorded 23.00 u of travel from (9343.642, 2786.733) to (9353.72, 2766.06) between t+112 s and t+117 s, at roughly 4.6 u/s - a normal walk. THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE: in the same minute the channel-1 body carried **1050 samples with 0 position changes**, and across 20:5x-21:0x there were **2 distinct claim values and 1 change**, which is a **243 u respawn jump**. CONCLUSION: **the `x,y` in the channel-1 body is a spawn/reference ANCHOR, not a live position feed.** It is updated on teleport and respawn, not by locomotion. It is 4.03 u from the accessor's value at spawn (the 'instrument offset' measured earlier), and it stays there while the player walks away. WHAT THIS INVALIDATES, and it has to be said plainly: (a) 'step 1: LEER the client's position from channel 1' was measuring an anchor. The field is real and readable; it is not the live position. (b) The desync detection that compared this claim against a constant server position was comparing two constants - which is why the error was EXACTLY 4.0311 u in every one of 2562 samples and calibrated to a residual of 0.0000. 'In sync' was trivially true and meant nothing. (c) The 3.342 u 'real divergence detected while walking' was the anchor drifting, not the player diverging. (d) The predictive simulator's 0.0419 u mean prediction error was measured on input that never moves, so it measured arithmetic on a constant. WHAT SURVIVES: the client DOES stream state 20 Hz on channel 1 (measured, 213k records), the camera yaw and pitch in that body are held state that changes when the player turns the camera, and the client's true position is readable through its own accessor - which is a client-side instrument, not a wire feed. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR SERVER AUTHORITY: the server cannot learn the player's live position from the wire as currently understood. Either another message carries it, or the authoritative position has to be derived from INPUT (which is not decoded) plus physics. That is a different and larger piece of work than 'read the claim and compare'.

CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-10-18, and this time the answer is complete: **the channel DOES carry the live position - in the movement BUFFER.** The conclusion above is right about the 311-byte form and wrong about the channel. The idle body is 311 bytes with ONE position (the anchor, which does not move). When the player moves the body GROWS to 403-412 bytes and carries a **sliding buffer of the last five movement samples, newest first, 20 Hz**. This project filtered for `len(payload) == 311` everywhere, so the anchor was all it ever saw. Verified against the client's own accessor polled at 20 Hz during a real 23 u walk: **600 of 600 buffer entries landed on the accessor's trajectory within 0.5 u**, across 120 messages. See `the_movement_buffer_is_the_live_position_feed_20261018`.

the_movement_buffer_is_the_live_position.what: MEASURED AND VALIDATED 2026-10-18. **The channel-1 body carries the player's live position as a sliding buffer of the last five movement samples.** This is the feed the whole project was looking for, and it was being filtered out. THE TWO FORMS:   idle  -> 311-byte payload, ONE position = the spawn anchor (does not follow the player)   moving -> 403-412-byte payload, FIVE positions, newest first, 0.051 s apart (20 Hz) Every analysis in this project filtered for `len(payload) == 311`, which is why the anchor was all it ever saw and why 'the channel carries no live position' looked true. LAYOUT: the buffer is anchored on the same `3d 4c cc cd` marker the idle form uses - first entry at marker+12, then ~63 bytes per further entry (64 for the first, so an index walk drifts; the reader searches a window after each entry). Each entry is `[f32be x][f32be y]` followed by a trailer whose last byte before the next entry is a DESCENDING input sequence number. VALIDATION, and it is the strongest in this project: the client's own position accessor (`frida-player-position`, which calls `FUN_140fddfa0` exactly as `nw_getPlayerPosition` does) was polled at 20 Hz while the player walked 23.00 u, and every buffer entry was matched against that trajectory. **600 of 600 entries across 120 messages landed within 0.5 u**, and entry-by-entry the timestamps form a clean 0.051 s ladder. THE FRAME OFFSET: `wire = accessor + (-2.2002, +3.3777)`, constant to 0.000 u - the same offset the anchor has, which is how the two forms were tied together. It is a FRAME difference between two quantities the client computes, not noise. The server stays in the WIRE frame (anchor, buffer and the state it writes back are all in it); the constant exists only to compare against the accessor. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROJECT: step 1 of the authority loop ('read the client's position') is now genuinely solved, and the server has a live feed to simulate from. The earlier correction that said otherwise was reading the idle form.

the_yaw_is_measured_from_plus_y_20261018.what: MEASURED 2026-10-18 on the live feed. The camera yaw in the channel-1 movement block is measured FROM +Y, not from +X, so the forward direction is `(-sin(yaw), cos(yaw))`. EVIDENCE: over 79 displacements during a real walk, `(movement heading - yaw)` is **+90.0 deg** in 77 of them and +90..+105 in the other 2. A constant 90 deg offset is the signature of a different angle origin, not of a noisy measurement. CROSS-CHECK: the measured yaw was -154.04 deg; `(-sin, cos)` of that is (0.438, -0.899), and the player's actual displacement over the walk was (10.1, -20.7) normalized = (0.439, -0.899). Exact. THE BUG THIS FIXED: the first implementation used `(cos, sin)`, the obvious reading, and it reported a player walking straight forward as walking sideways - forward_speed 0.00 u/s, lateral_speed +3.83 u/s on a plain W walk. After the fix the same data reads forward 3.83 u/s, lateral 0.00. The class had been 'working' and reporting the opposite of the truth. MEASURED STATE AFTER THE FIX, on 133 real walking samples: forward 3.83 u/s median, lateral 0.00, mean prediction error **0.1265 u**, 0 violations, 0 disagreements.

the_server_now_enforces_movement_authori.va: services/world/src/azoth_world/movement.py::CorrectionPolicy, CorrectionAction, CorrectionDecision; rep.py::_observe_movement_claim, maybe_state_stream; levers AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FREEZE_AFTER, AZOTH_MOVEMENT_DISCONNECT_AFTER, AZOTH_MOVEMENT_SUMMARY_PERIOD_S
the_server_now_enforces_movement_authori.what: IMPLEMENTED AND VERIFIED LIVE 2026-10-18. **The world server now enforces movement authority on its own, and a live run shows it following a real walk with zero corrections.** THE ARCHITECTURE, from the client's own cvars rather than guessed: the CLIENT owns its locomotion and corrects its own desync (`javelin.alc-correct-position-desync-*`), while the SERVER validates and reacts (`javelin-server.alc-speed-hack-fix-v2-wipe-inputs`, `player-teleport-2d-distance-metrics-threshold`). So a correction is the server refusing or limiting what it accepts - NOT pushing a position, which this build has no working channel for (`IPositionReceiver`'s apply is `ret 0`, measured). THE LAYERS, deliberately separate so each is testable without a running game:   1. alc.read_live_position  - the client's live position (movement buffer, validated 600/600)   2. MovementSimulator / YawAwareSimulator - the server's OWN position + prediction   3. CorrectionPolicy        - what the server DOES about a divergence THE ESCALATION, gradual because a single bad claim is normal (a lag spike, a dropped input):   ACCEPT      claim plausible, adopted   HOLD        keep the server's position, do not adopt; divergence recorded   FREEZE      past `freeze_after` violations, stop refreshing the player state stream - MEASURED 2026-10-13 to freeze the client's simulation and make W do nothing, so it IS a real lever and the strongest one short of disconnecting   DISCONNECT  past `disconnect_after` violations, drop a client that will not converge   and it RECOVERS: `recover_after` clean samples resume the stream VERIFIED LIVE (run 22:00): the server's own position tracked a real 23.02 u walk from (9341.44, 2790.11) to (9352.11, 2769.72) with **adopted 3317, violations 0, mean prediction error 0.0027 u**, 3 decisions all ACCEPT, and the client reported 0 `Failed to unmarshal`, 0 `ValidationError`, 0 `transportError`, 0 connection warnings. **A legitimate walk produces zero corrections** - which is the correct behaviour and the thing a naive authoritative server gets wrong by rubber-banding an honest player. A BUG FOUND AND FIXED WHILE WIRING IT: `set_offset` clears the tracker's streak (correct - a new frame invalidates a streak built in the old one), and it was being called on EVERY sample, so the streak reset forever and the desync never fired. Now called once. SECOND BUG: `movement-simulation-held` logged once per sample because it shared a dedup flag with the validator, whose reference resets after a rejection and then reports the next sample as its own first sample. It has its own flag now.

the_freeze_lever_is_proven_live_20261019.va: rep.py::MOVEMENT_FORCE, movement_force_spec, _observe_movement_claim; movement.py::CorrectionPolicy; lever AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FORCE, AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FORCE_FILE, AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FREEZE_AFTER
the_freeze_lever_is_proven_live_20261019.what: PROVEN LIVE 2026-10-19, twice. **Withholding the player state stream stops the client's simulation.** This was the last unproven rung of the correction ladder: an honest client never claims impossible movement, so HOLD/FREEZE/DISCONNECT could never fire by just playing. THE PROVOCATION LEVER: `AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FORCE=1` + `AZOTH_MOVEMENT_FORCE_FILE` moves the SERVER's position out from under the client, which makes the client's next claim diverge by construction. The file is re-read every sample, so a test moves the server mid-session without a restart. Off by default; it exists only to observe the ladder. THE LADDER FIRED IN ORDER, both runs: HOLD at 1 violation -> FREEZE at 5 -> DISCONNECT at the configured cap (200 in run 1, 1000 in run 2). THE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT, run 2, with W HELD THROUGH THE WHOLE WINDOW:   06:59:00  409 B  (9341.8, 2789.3)  21 distinct positions  <- walking   06:59:01  405 B  (9344.4, 2784.1)  19 distinct            <- walking   06:59:02  405 B  (9346.6, 2779.5)  20 distinct            <- walking   06:59:03  405 B  (9349.0, 2774.5)  20 distinct            <- FREEZE fired (viol 5)   06:59:04  403 B  (9351.4, 2769.6)   6 distinct            <- decelerating   06:59:05  408 B  (9351.5, 2769.4)   1 distinct            <- FROZEN   06:59:06+ 120 B  (9351.5, 2769.4)   1 distinct            <- body collapsed, for good W stayed held until 06:59:13 - EIGHT SECONDS of continued input - and the player did not move a millimetre. The channel-1 payload also collapsed from the ~405-byte moving form to a **120-byte** form and stayed there: the client stopped streaming movement state, not merely stopped changing position. THE CLIENT SURVIVED: 0 `transportError`, 0 `Disconnected from REP`, 0 `Cleanup()`. It logged 13 `State(InGame) is timeout : frames 10` - the InGame watchdog firing because the state stream stopped, which is the expected symptom and independent corroboration that the stream is what was withheld. WHY THIS MATTERS: it converts the correction ladder from a unit-tested design into a measured behaviour. The server can now stop a client that will not converge, and the evidence that it did is the client's own frozen position while its input was still held.

the_server_can_move_a_world_entity_and_e.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-19, and the live run is what produced both halves of the result. **(1) THE SERVER CAN MOVE AN ENTITY IN THE WORLD, AND THE CLIENT OBEYS.** With `AZOTH_SERVER_ENTITY=1` and a target position, the server rewrote a captured entity's position in the state it sends. The entity was record 70 (a STRUCTURE). When the server moved it to the player's own position, the player ended up STANDING ON A HOUSE that had not been there - collision included. So the write path works end to end: the server decided a world entity's position and the client applied it. **(2) THE FIRST ATTEMPT PICKED THE WRONG KIND OF ENTITY, and the mistake is instructive.** Record 70 has **2 fragments** and a 162-byte payload: a structure. A character carries many components (records 29/30/60/79/87/88/89/90/91/92/93/94 have 16-21 fragments). Moving a 2-fragment record relocates a prop; it does not produce a person. **(3) AN ENTITY'S POSITION IS NOT AT A FIXED OFFSET.** Measured across records: payload offset 6 for records 82/80/78/77/76/24/85/70, and offset **238** for record 29. `template_from_replay` therefore finds it BY VALUE - the first plausible world coordinate - and records how many times that exact pair occurs so the rewrite can refuse a body whose layout differs. `replace_entity_position` then rewrites the pair wherever it appears, which covers BOTH records of one entity: record 68 (seq 0x7a) CREATES an entity and carries the pair at 159/227, record 70 (seq 0xb0) UPDATES it at 6/74 - and the creation record is below the stream floor, so patching only the update record moved nothing. That was the second mistake, and it is why the first live attempt showed no change at all. **(4) HOW ENTITY CREATION ACTUALLY WORKS, now identified.** `ClientAddEntryMsg` (wire 0xa4, 20 bytes) is `[00 01][a4][16-byte actor id]` - the capture sends it twice, before the spawn, and the actor id it registers is the player's. Entity records carry **component GUIDs, not actor ids** (record 29 does not contain the player's actor id; the spawn record does, once). So creating an entity is TWO steps: register an actor id, then send a record carrying that actor's component state. WHAT IS NOT DONE: a NEW npc. Moving a captured entity works; inventing one needs a new actor id, a `ClientAddEntryMsg` for it, and a record whose fragments carry that actor's components - and the per-component payload codecs are still undecoded, which is the long tail the replication architecture note describes. The honest next step is to take a captured CHARACTER record (29 has 19 fragments and sits 5.8 u from the player), register a second actor id, and replicate that record twice under two identities - not to compose a character from nothing.

the_inventory_response_is_decoded_and_a_.what:
DECODED AND A REAL BUG FIXED, 2026-10-19. (1) THE RESPONSE IS DECODED. `InventoriesComponentClientFacet_OnQueryInventories` (wire 0x16a0) has two captured bodies: **153 B** (the empty form, no entries) and **99 819 B** (the populated one, **428 entries**). The body is `[00 01][a0 5a][16-byte target][01][varint 0x16c4][...]` then `entry x N`. Each entry is anchored by the marker `00 01 82 5a` **68 bytes into it**, and holds, in order: a NUL-padded container name (`w-world|`), the marker, a varint length, the item type name (`SkinCollection`), a 16-byte GUID, 4 flag bytes, the literal `isCollected`, a 4-byte count, a `0x02` tag, a length byte and the item id as DECIMAL ASCII (`1027224182`). (2) THE SIZE VARIES, AND THAT IS THE TRAP. An entry is **223 + id_length** bytes: measured **233** for a 10-digit id (338 entries), **232** for 9 digits (79), **231** for 8 (10). A parser assuming a fixed stride reads 19 of 428 entries and then walks into padding - which the first attempt did. The walk must anchor on the marker. (3) ROUND-TRIP IS BYTE-IDENTICAL: re-rendering the parsed entries reproduces the 99 819-byte capture exactly, which is what makes it safe to change one id and send the result. (4) A REAL BUG IN THE EXISTING GATING, found while wiring this. `RESPONSE_REQUESTS[0x16A0]` was `(0x169D,)`, so `_deferred_decision` held both inventory responses and then dropped them as `request-not-seen`. But the client **never sends 0x169D**: 0 of 39 client messages in the committed capture, and 0 `inbound-typed` 0x169D events in any live session. The REAL server sent 0x16A0 at seq 0x28 and 0x29 **unsolicited**, and the client accepted both. So the rule required a request that cannot arrive and suppressed a legitimate push. Corrected to the empty tuple ("no request required"), with a test that asserts the capture has no such request and that the real server sent the response anyway. (5) THE SERVER CAN NOW COMPOSE IT: `compose_inventory_body` re-renders the response from a list of item ids (`AZOTH_INVENTORY_IDS_FILE`, one per line) using the captured body as the template, so every undecoded header byte stays exactly as the client produced it. Off by default (`AZOTH_INVENTORY_COMPOSE=0`); a non-numeric id is skipped rather than written as garbage. NOT CLAIMED: the MEANING of the fields. Which flag bit does what, whether the numeric id is a database key or a counter, and what the `0x02` tag is, are all undecoded - the module carries them through unchanged rather than inventing them.

LIVE RESULT 2026-10-19 (run 09:05): the gating fix and the composition BOTH work, and the UI does not open. Measured in one session with `AZOTH_INVENTORY_COMPOSE=1` and a 3-id file:   * `0x16a0` suppressed: **0** in that session (was 2 per session before the fix)   * both bodies sent: seq 40 (153 B, the empty form) and seq 41 (**99 819 B, 91 chunks**)   * `server-inventory-composed`: entries 428, **changed 3**, size 99 819   * client: **0** `Failed to unmarshal`, 0 `ValidationError`, 0 `transportError`, 0 connection warnings, and **0** log lines mentioning inventory   * input demonstrably reaches the client: holding W moved the player 9341.44 -> 9348.67 So the server composed a 99 819-byte inventory with three rewritten item ids, sent it, and the client parsed it without complaint. ****ACCEPTANCE MET**: TAB opens the inventory and it renders the 428 entries, with armour, weapons, rewards, jewellery, reagents and pelts - the body the server composed. The first attempt failed only because of HOW the key was sent (see `synthetic_keys_must_use_scan_codes_not_vk_20261019`). WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN: it does not mean the composition is wrong - a parse error would be logged and none is. It means the UI needs something else, and the two candidates are (a) the keybind differs in this build or the synthetic key does not reach the UI layer (W does, so the game receives input, but a UI panel may require the window to be focused differently), or (b) the client's inventory facet needs a readiness/ownership step before it will render - `InventoriesComponentServerFacet_ReadyRegionalOwnerData` (0x1686) and `..._ReadyGlobalOwnerData` (0x169f) exist in the registry and were never sent by the capture. The next experiment is (b): send those two readiness messages and see whether the UI opens.

FINAL LIVE RESULT 2026-10-19 (run 09:20): with the key sent as a SCAN CODE, **TAB opens the inventory and it is populated** - armour slots, weapons, rewards, jewellery, reagents, pelts, weight `90/91.90`, gold `2.492`. `server-inventory-composed` logged entries 428, changed 3, size 99 819; 0 `0x16a0` suppressed; 0 `Failed to unmarshal`, 0 `ValidationError`, 0 `transportError`. **The server composed a 99 819-byte inventory with three rewritten item ids and the client rendered it.**

synthetic_keys_must_use_scan_codes_not_v.what: MEASURED 2026-10-19, and it cost a false negative. `scripts/send-input.py` sends a VIRTUAL KEY CODE through SendInput **without** `KEYEVENTF_SCANCODE`. `scripts/hold-key.py` sends a real **SCAN CODE** with that flag. client_slot_table_measured_1_to_94_occup.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-19 with `reverse/probes/client/frida-record-slots.py`, and it corrects a project assumption that had been used to choose an entity's record id. THE TABLE: `state + 0x608 + record_id*0x10`, read for every id 0..255. **Ids 1..94 are all non-NULL and 95..255 are all NULL** - a contiguous allocated range, which is what a handler table built once at world load looks like. THE CORRECTION: `entities.CAPTURED_RECORD_IDS` was derived by reading only the FIRST record of each captured payload, and a payload is a SEQUENCE of records (`[u8 id][u8 frags][fragments...]`, repeated) that cannot be walked because a fragment carries no length field. So that set is a **lower bound**, not the occupied set, and choosing a 'free' id from it picked **slot 3 - which is allocated**. The consequence was measured, not inferred: the dispatcher reported `slotEmpty: false` for slot 3 on every send, i.e. the message was an UPDATE, which the first-write-wins component maps discard (`component_map_is_first_write_wins_20261018`). That is why the first two duplication attempts produced no second body while every counter stayed clean. `entities.MEASURED_USED_SLOTS` now carries the measured set, `free_record_ids()` starts at **95**, and `AZOTH_NPC_DUPLICATE=auto` resolves to it; an allocated id is refused at load with a log line instead of being sent as a silently-dropped update.

The client's gate drops any unreliable replication whose counter is not strictly greater than `port[+0x78]`, and on a live session that high-water was **1216** - so **every** NPC bundle was discarded before reaching the record dispatcher. The probe proved the discard rather than assuming it: of 81 distinct record ids arriving at `FUN_141717fc0`, **95 was not among them**, while the server logged a send every second. AFTER THE FIX (the NPC body now goes through `javelin_bundle.with_replication_seq` on the SAME monotone counter the state stream uses) the wire shows the counter advancing (`018e0e`/`01930e`/`01990e` = 1806/1811/1817) and **record 95 reaches the dispatcher**. So both bugs were real, both were measured, and the second was invisible until the first was fixed.

With both bugs fixed (a genuinely free slot, 95, and an advancing replication counter) record 95 **does** reach the dispatcher, and slot 95 **does** become non-NULL - so the creation path is being entered. the_created_entity_does_not_render_and_t.what: NEGATIVE RESULT, MEASURED 2026-10-19 with a controlled A/B, and it retracts a candidate reading before it became a claim. THE STATE OF THE MECHANISM: with both bugs fixed - a genuinely free record slot (95, from the client's own table) and a replication counter that advances past the client's high-water - record 95 **reaches** `FUN_141717fc0`, slot 95 **becomes non-NULL**, and with a SINGLE send the slot is **STABLE** (1 distinct pointer in 9 timed samples), whereas re-sending the 19-fragment record once per second made it CHURN (a new pointer on every dispatch, 1:1 with the dispatch count, while slots 89..94 stayed stable). ACCEPTANCE FOR 'a NEW actor, not a moved one' IS THEREFORE NOT MET: two bodies where there was one were NOT demonstrated. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: the actor id is a real, addressable field inside the record (16 bytes at payload offset 662 in record 29, same shape as the player's at 29731 in the spawn record); it can be rewritten with exactly 16 bytes differing; `ClientAddEntryMsg` is composed byte-exactly; the record now passes the replication gate and is dispatched; and the slot is created and stable. WHAT IS MISSING is the last step - the client builds something in that slot but does not produce a visible body. The next instrument is the actor/entity table (`FUN_146801040`, manager at `this+0x110`) counted before and after, plus a hook on the creation apply `FUN_14178db00` to see whether it is reached for slot 95 and what it returns - not another payload shape.

gathering_has_no_client_to_server_reques.va: not a VA: the AZ type registry (research/atlas/az-type-registry.json, build 8654f01d…) filtered for Gathering/Gatherable/Interactor with in_type_table true
gathering_has_no_client_to_server_reques.what: STATIC NEGATIVE, measured 2026-10-19, and it REFUTES the premise the roadmap item was written on. The roadmap says 'an interaction is an RMI on a component facet. Pick one gatherable, decode its request from a live session, answer it authoritatively.' **There is no client->server gathering request to decode.** The whole Gathering/Gatherable family in the type table is: `GatherableControllerComponentClientFacet_GatheringInterrupted` (0xaa4), `…_RequestOpenStorage` (0x1b45), `…_StartEmoteGathering` (0x1448), `GatheringComponentClientFacet_OnEnteredProximityGatherable` (0x13d6), `…_OnExitedProximityGatherable` (0x13fe), `…_OnResourcesNotGranted` (0x1b1d), `…_StartEmoteGathering` (0x144b) - **all ClientFacet, i.e. the SERVER calling the CLIENT** - and exactly ONE ServerFacet message, `GatherableControllerComponentServerFacet_SetStateDebugClient` (0x353), which is a DEBUG setter and not a gameplay request. The Interactor family is the same shape: every non-debug `InteractorComponentServerFacet_*` is TERRITORY governance (rosters, projects, signups, taxes), not interaction with a world object, and the only interaction-ish request in the whole registry is `InteractorComponentServerFacet_RequestRemoteInteract` (0x13af) plus `PlayerHousingComponentServerFacet_InteractWithHousingItem` (0xe92). WHAT THIS MEANS, and it is the same lesson the movement work already taught: **the client's gathering is client-authoritative and the server is told by REPLICATED STATE, not by a request.** `GatherableControllerComponent` and `GatheringComponent` both have `InitializeReplicatedFields` in their ServerFacet (found in the image strings), which is the same signature that made `PositionInTheWorldComponent` travel as replicated state rather than as an RMI (`position_state_may_arrive_as_replicated_state_not_rmi_20261012`). So 'answer the request' is not implementable, and the roadmap item must be re-scoped to: find which record/fragment carries `GatherableControllerComponentReplicatedState` / `GatheringComponentReplicatedState`, which is the state a gatherable's depletion would have to be expressed in. THE CHEAP CONFIRMING MEASUREMENT (not yet done, needs a live session): have the player chop a tree and read `inbound-typed` - if no gathering type appears, the negative is confirmed live. `INBOUND_KNOWN_REQUESTS` now names 0x13af and 0xe92 so that such a session names them instead of logging an unknown type.

gathering_sends_no_request_the_client_re.va: not a VA: live measurement, world server `inbound-typed` events during a real gathering action; session 2026-10-19T13:25:38Z (client pid 11932)
gathering_sends_no_request_the_client_re.what: MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-19, and it CONFIRMS the static negative (`gathering_has_no_client_to_server_request_message_20261019`) with the strongest possible evidence: the operator walked to a plant, pressed gather, and reported that **the character would not stop gathering**. Over that action the server received **exactly ONE typed client message: `0x1910` (6416), 78 bytes**, and **no gathering, gatherable or interaction type at all** - not 0x13af (`InteractorComponentServerFacet_RequestRemoteInteract`), not 0xe92, not any `Gathering*` wire type. The single message is `TerritoryDetectorComponentServerFacet_AttemptTerritoryExit`, resolved by the descriptor adjacency method (name -> 6 NUL bytes -> `{GUID}` at file offset 0x80f5e90, GUID `8979AFE6-8195-46C7-96FF-CE28785678F0`, type-table index 6416 in `private-client/runtime/typeindex.json`), i.e. unrelated to gathering. WHY THE CHARACTER WOULD NOT STOP: the client is the authority for gathering and repeats the action because **nothing on the server side ever confirms or advances it**. This is the gathering analogue of the movement finding - the client owns the behaviour and the server is expected to reflect it back as state - and it explains the symptom exactly, without needing a request that does not exist. WHAT THIS CLOSES AND WHAT IT OPENS: the roadmap's framing ('decode its request from a live session, answer it authoritatively') is now measured to be unimplementable - there is no request. What a gatherable's depletion has to be expressed in is REPLICATED STATE (`GatherableControllerComponentReplicatedState` / `GatheringComponentReplicatedState`, both of which have `InitializeReplicatedFields` in their ServerFacet), i.e. the same record/fragment mechanism as the player's position. The next experiment is therefore: find which record id / fragment key carries the gatherable's replicated state in the spawn record and whether the server can write it - and the repeated-gathering symptom is the acceptance signal, because a confirmed gatherable should stop repeating.

the_client_cannot_bind_a_transform_to_re.what: MEASURED 2026-10-19, and it is the most important negative in this session because it explains BOTH the created entity and the second-player item at once. **The client logs `Slice: Couldn't get Transform component on the slice!` for `slices/remoteplayer.dynamicslice` (asset `A660EEEB-EBC7-5CB7-BE6B-AB11EB831731:64`) on EVERY session, and that is the SAME slice whose instance carries every entity's actor id** - the GUID embedded in record 29 at payload offset 642 is exactly `a660eeebebc75cb7be6bab11eb831731`. Counts in one clean session with the NPC feature **DISABLED**: 26 warnings, all at 13:28:00.457, i.e. 5 s after `player spawn succeeds` at 13:27:55.506, and the replay declares **46 slice instances across 13 record ids** (1, 29, 30, 60, 79, 87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94) - the remote players and creatures. WHY THIS MATTERS, and it is a pre-existing condition rather than anything this session broke: the static chain recorded in `gametransform_entity_attach` already says the class map the slice clone uses never receives `GameTransformComponent` from any function that runs at startup (`FUN_141582430` is the only inserter and its only caller `FUN_141763b70` has no static callers), so **the cloned remote-entity entities have a null Transform slot**. A slice instance without a Transform has no world matrix, so it cannot be placed in the scene - which is exactly 'the actor exists in the client's tables but no body is drawn'. CONSEQUENCES, stated as consequences and not as proof: (1) the entity-creation work is very likely blocked by this and not by the record's contents, which is consistent with every measured fact - the record is dispatched, the slot is created and stable, the bytes are the client's own, and still no body; (2) the second-player item is blocked by the SAME thing, because a remote player IS one of these slice instances, so it must not be started until this is resolved. repairing_the_transform_removed_26_warni.what: MEASURED 2026-10-19, and it is a HONEST MIXED RESULT: one symptom was removed and a new one was created, so this is NOT a fix. WHAT WORKED. Hooking it and rewriting the RETURN VALUE to a freshly built GameTransform made the client's own count go **26 warnings -> 0**: `attached=26` and `Couldn't get Transform component` vanished from Game.log. That proves the repair reaches the caller, which the earlier attempt did not: installing the component with AddComponent alone left `attached=26` AND all 26 warnings, because the caller tests `rax` and the log line is emitted after the return. The warning count is therefore a valid instrument for this. WHAT BROKE, and it is why this is recorded as a negative: in the SAME session the 26 Transform warnings were replaced by **26 `[ERROR] Slice: The slice has more than one root. Undefined behavior may occur with messaging.`** lines at the same timestamp. So handing a default-constructed transform back to the clone path does not place the entity; it makes the slice have two roots. (3) One run attached the probe to TWO NewWorld processes because the old client had not been stopped first, and its counters reset mid-session - a session in that state is invalid. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE ENTITY WORK: the missing Transform is real and is now provably repairable, but the repair has to satisfy the slice's root structure, not just supply a matrix. The next experiment is NOT another cap or another retval write: it is to find what the slice instantiation expects to own the root (the atlas already records that the clone path never receives GameTransformComponent at startup and that FUN_141582430 is the only inserter), and to install the component BEFORE the clone instead of patching the lookup's answer afterwards.

the_transform_gate_runs_30_times_and_its.what: MEASURED 2026-10-19, and it LOCALISES the Transform gap to a single virtual call instead of leaving it as 'the clone map is never seeded'. THE CHAIN, from the decompiled `FUN_141763b70` (the gate): `if (param_1) { lVar10 = param_1->vtable[+0x20](param_1, FUN_1407fbe80()); } if (lVar10 != 0) { FUN_141582430(lVar10, ...); }` - and `FUN_141582430` is the ONLY function in the image that inserts `{484AE67D-ABD0-4D9C-B2C8-9BB0EEC900E0}` GameTransformComponent into the class map the slice clone reads. So registration happens exactly when that interface lookup returns non-null. THE MEASUREMENT (probe `frida-transform-gate`, attached before world load, 555129 component lookups confirming a live session): **gate = 30 calls, register = 0 calls.** The gate function DOES run - once per slice, with **30 distinct job pointers** (0x201fb7b2800, 0x201fd226800, ... 0x201fdbc6c00) - and `FUN_141582430` is **never reached**. Therefore the interface lookup `vtable[+0x20](job, typeId)` returns NULL for every one of the 30 slices, and the class map is never seeded. WHY THIS IS THE ANSWER THE EARLIER WORK WAS MISSING: the atlas recorded 'the class map never receives GameTransformComponent from any function that runs at startup' as a static conclusion, and separately measured 26 null Transform lookups per session. Those two facts are now joined by a runtime count: the one function that could seed the map IS called, and its precondition fails. The fix is therefore NOT to reach the gate (it is already reached) and NOT to patch the lookup's answer (tried 2026-10-19: it turned 26 warnings into 26 `The slice has more than one root` errors and an APPCRASH in NewWorld.exe). The fix is at `vtable[+0x20]` on the slice job object: find why the interface is not implemented for those 30 objects. WHAT REMAINS UNPROVEN: that seeding the class map would produce a body. It would make the 26 lookups succeed through the client's OWN path (a real Transform built by the clone, with a proper root) rather than a default-constructed one handed back afterwards, which is precisely the difference that made the lookup patch break the slice's root structure. That is the next experiment, and it is the one with the best chance of producing a visible second body.

the_gate_interface_83482f97_is_partly_un.what: MEASURED 2026-10-19, and the FIRST VERSION OF THIS RECORD WAS PARTLY WRONG - corrected here rather than deleted, because the correction is the useful part. WHAT IS SOLID. The gate calls `param_1->vtable[+0x20](param_1, FUN_1407fbe80())`. `FUN_1407fbe80` (decompiled) is a TLS-cached type-id getter built from the descriptor at `UNK_147f02048`, whose bytes are the ASCII GUID **`{83482F97-84DA-4FD4-BF9E-7FE34C8E091F}`** - so that GUID is the type id the gate asks for. The descriptor appears exactly once in the image (file 0x7f00849) and its slot table, read at pad=1 with **6 of 6** entries landing on real code, is: `+0x00 = 0x1402f0e20` (constructor), `+0x08 = 0x140294860`, `+0x10 = 0x140294860`, `+0x18 = 0x14143a8b0`, `+0x20 = 0x14143acd0`, `+0x28 = 0x140294860`. `0x140294860` disassembles to **`ret 0`**, so three of those six slots are unimplemented stubs. WHAT THE FIRST VERSION GOT WRONG, and it matters: it implied that `+0x20` being a stub is why the gate gets null. It is NOT - `+0x20` here is `0x14143acd0`, a real function. More importantly, **this is the INTERFACE DESCRIPTOR's slot table, not the table the gate dispatches through.** The gate calls `*(code**)(*param_1 + 0x20)` on the SLICE JOB object, so the QueryInterface it reaches belongs to the job's own vtable, and this descriptor only supplies the type id it passes IN. Reading the descriptor's slots and concluding anything about the gate's result was a category error. WHAT REMAINS ESTABLISHED AND USEFUL: (1) the exact type id the gate requests, `{83482F97-...}`, which is the thing to look for in the runtime query; (2) that this build carries `ret 0` stubs in this area at all, consistent with the two earlier stub findings (`IPositionReceiver`'s apply and the RMI facet path), so 'the interface is not fully implemented' is a live hypothesis rather than a wild one; (3) the runtime count from the other record - gate runs 30 times, `FUN_141582430` registers 0 times. THE NEXT MEASUREMENT, which is now unambiguous: dump the vtable of the 30 job objects at runtime and disassemble the slot at `+0x20` for each, then call it and see what it returns for `{83482F97-...}`. That is a direct answer, and it does not depend on any alignment guess.
